extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: A compendium of legal principles and case-based standards governing patent coverage, infringement, remedies (especially injunctions and bonds), liability of parties, interference practice, and standards for patentability and inventive skill. Intended as a practitioner's reference to evaluate claims, defenses, and procedural posture in patent disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement to equivalents despite reformed claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee is entitled to equivalents though he may have reformed his claims under requirements of the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Rodebaugh v. Jackson (1889). Principle: narrowing or amending claims during prosecution does not necessarily deprive the patentee of protection under the doctrine of equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel of attorney-in-fact who conveys patent
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney in fact, conveying the patent under a power, is not estopped to deny validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: H. Tibbe & Son Mfg. Co. v. Heineker (1889). Practical: assignment/transfer by agent does not automatically bar later challenges to validity by transferee.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an improvement constitutes a new species
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation of an improvement to its original is not always that of species to a genus; a species is created only when an original generic element is supplanted by a new or modified element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Ex parte Smith (1888). Use to determine whether an improvement is a distinct invention or merely a variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process vs apparatus are distinct inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A process and its apparatus are not genus and species but distinct inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Ex parte Atwood (1888). Implication: separate patent protection and infringement analyses may apply to process claims and apparatus claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater perfection does not negate identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater perfection in the result effected does not show want of identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: MacDonald v. McLean (1889). Applied when accused device is an improved version but performs the same identified function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use for a different purpose can be infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the invention for a different purpose is infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Thompson v. Gildersleeve (1888). Even non-ordinary uses that fall within claim scope may infringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of part to authorized users not infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale of part of an invention to those who have a right to use it is not an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Morgan Envelope Co. v. Albany Perforated Wrapping Paper Co. (1889). Distinguished from supplying components to infringers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of element with innocent use does not infringe combination
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale of an element capable of an innocent use, and without collusion, does not infringe the patent for the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Winne v. Bedell (1889). Focus on intent and knowledge; component capable of substantial noninfringing uses is protected absent evidence of contributory intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint infringement is one tort; satisfaction against one bars others
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint infringement is one tort, and recovery of satisfaction against one tort-feasor is a bar to further proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Babcock & Wilcox Co. v. Pioneer Iron Works (1888). Coordination among co-defendants and finality considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate acts by different parties can infringe if common purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be infringed by the separate acts of different parties having a common purpose, though no one act is by itself an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. American Zylonite Co. (1887). Used in multi-actor scenarios where combined conduct achieves claim elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement treated as improvement when patents unified
rubrics_metrics.description: When the titles to two conflicting patents are united in one owner, one invention may be treated as an improvement on the other as against an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Putnam v. Keystone Bottle Stopper Co. (1889). Fusion of titles affects enforcement strategy and claim interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: User under two patents liable for uncovered aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: Where two patents cover in part the same field, a party who has used under both may be held liable for that in each which was not covered by the other, and cannot claim the later was void because anticipated by the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Deane v. Hodge (1886). Limits on asserting cross-invalidity as a defense to liability under multiple patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination patent: substance taken infringes despite equivalents/changes
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination-patent is infringed if the substance of the combination is taken, whatever equivalents, alterations, or omissions may be resorted to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Proctor v. Bennis (1887). Courts look to whether accused device appropriates the heart of the claimed cooperative arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination not infringed unless all elements or equivalents used
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination is not infringed unless all its elements or their equivalents are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Perkins v. Eaton (1889). Defense: absence of one claim element or its equivalent defeats infringement of the combination claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking some elements with equivalents for others can infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking some of the elements with equivalents for the others infringes the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Leary v. Hohenstein (1889). Equivalents analysis may make up for altered elements when overall function/substance is appropriated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction after patent expiry not infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The reconstruction of a combination after its patent has expired is not an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Johnson v. Brooklyn & C.R. Co. (1888). Post-expiration rebuilding of earlier patented products is permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent for an art not infringed if some steps omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for an art is not infringed if some of its steps are omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Royer v. Coupe (1889). Process claims require performance of claimed steps (or their equivalents) to constitute infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process infringed by employing essence regardless of apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: A process is infringed by employing the essence of the invention, whatever apparatus may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Morley Mach. Co. v. Lancaster (1889). Courts focus on the substantive method/essence rather than precise mechanical implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine patent infringement by means-to-result equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine performing new functions is infringed by any mechanism which employs the same means to accomplish the same results, though its parts are individually improved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Morley Mach. Co. v. Lancaster. Improver cannot avoid infringement by improving individual parts if the accused device uses same means to same ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent may be infringed even if infringer's name attached
rubrics_metrics.description: A design may infringe though the infringer's name be coupled with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Redway v. Ohio Stove Co. (1889). Attribution/branding does not avoid design infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government use measured by implied contract absent special agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: In absence of any special agreement, the acts of the government in using an invention measure its liability under an implied contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Butler v. United States (1888). Government immunity limited; remedies under implied contract principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized use by public officer does not create implied contract to pay
rubrics_metrics.description: The unauthorized use of an invention by a public officer does not raise an implied contract on the part of the government to pay for such use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Forehand v. United States (1888). Distinguish authorized procurement vs unauthorized acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government denial of ownership defeats contract theory
rubrics_metrics.description: When the government denies that the invention used is the property of the claimant, the use is not under a contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Schillinger v. United States (1889). Practical effect on recovery against government.

rubrics_metrics.name: City may be liable for contractor's infringement under its orders
rubrics_metrics.description: A city may be liable for an infringement committed by a contractor acting under its orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Asbestine Tiling & Mfg. Co. v. Hepp (1889). Municipal liability when acts are done under municipal direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers of solvent corporation not personally liable absent participation
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer of a solvent corporation is not liable for its infringements unless he personally participates therein, though he may be bound by an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Boston Woven Hose Co. v. Star Rubber Co. (1889). Remedies target corporate entity; individual relief limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers not individually enjoined where corporation solvent absent personal violation
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers of a corporation though made parties will not be individually enjoined or ordered to account when the corporation is solvent, unless they as individuals have violated or threaten to violate the patentee's rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Howard v. St. Paul Plow Works (1888). Equity will not pierce corporate veil without individual culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensor equity liability for licensee acts following licensor directions
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensor is liable in equity for infringing acts committed by his licensees when following his directions and working drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Toppan v. Tiffany Refrigerator Car Co. (1889). Active participation/direction by licensor creates liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee exceeding scope becomes an infringer
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee exceeding his license becomes an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Covell v. Bostwick (1889). Key: scope-of-license analysis controls liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee under one claim may infringe another claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee under one claim of a patent may be treated as an infringer of another claim, though the infringement is accomplished by the use of the licensed claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: United Nickel Co. v. California Electrical Works (1885). Cross-claim infringement liability may arise despite an existing license for a different claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workman without pecuniary interest not an infringer
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere workman having no pecuniary interest in the product of his labor is not an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Young v. Foerster (1889). Focus on intent and benefit rather than mere performance of tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement action survives against executor
rubrics_metrics.description: An action in equity for infringement survives against the executor of the infringer, although no injunction can be granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Hohorst v. Howard (1888). Executors may be liable for accounting/damages even if injunction relief not available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement must be proved, not conjectured
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement must be proved, not conjectured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Winne v. Bedell (1889); Morgan Envelope Co. (1889). Burden on plaintiff to present admissible proof of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction refused without judgments/acquiescence/success in interference
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be refused in the absence of judgments, acquiescence, or success in an interference proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Edward Barr Co. v. N.Y. & N.H. Automatic Sprinkler Co. (1887). Court discretion to deny preliminary relief where entitlement is uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction refused when infringement doubtful
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be refused when there are no judgments or acquiescence, and infringement is doubtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Baymond v. Boston Woven Hose Co. (1889). High standard of likelihood of success required for equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction refused where plaintiff guilty of laches and defendant solvent would be greatly injured
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be refused when there are no judgments or acquiescence, and defendant is solvent and would sustain great injury, and the plaintiff has been guilty of laches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Hurlburt v. Carter (1889). Equity balances harm and plaintiff's delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction refused when plaintiff recently acquired patent and defendant has long business
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be refused where no judgments or acquiescence, the infringement is denied, and defendants are pecuniarily responsible, and have a long time carried on an extensive business, while plaintiff has owned the patent but a few months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Johnson v. Aldrich (1889). Courts consider relative equities and business disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraining order can be granted on prior judgments and public acquiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: A restraining order, pending trial, will be granted on one final judgment and several interlocutory orders for injunctions and a public acquiescence of several years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Schneider v. Missouri Glass Co. (1888). Strong prior judicial support and industry acquiescence favor injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may order issue at law before injunction if validity doubtful
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction may issue without a prior judgment at law, but the court, if validity is doubtful, may order an issue at law before allowing an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Wise v. Grand Avenue R.R. Co. (1888). Courts sometimes require adjudication of validity before equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction refused where plaintiff's supporting judgment is under appeal and defendant acted in good faith
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be refused where the evidence of validity consists of a judgment from which an appeal is pending, and where the defendant is acting in good faith and in ignorance of the infringement and would sustain irreparable injury, while the plaintiff has an adequate remedy at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Consolidated Roller Mill Co. v. Richmond City Mill Works (1889). Pending higher-court appeal weakens request for injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction refused where defendants deny validity and no judgment equivalent exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there has been no judgment or its equivalent, and the defendants deny the validity of the patent if so construed as to prohibit their acts, an injunction will be refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Dickerson v. De La Vergne Refrigerating Mach. Co. (1888). Disputed validity mitigates against preliminary equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence implies adverse interest and submission to patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquiescence implies an interest adverse to the patent and a submission to the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Raymond v. Boston Woven Hose Co. (1889). Acquiescence affects laches and equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence in several patents not acquiescence in any single patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquiescence in the right of the inventor to an invention covered by several patents is not acquiescence in any one patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Upton v. Wayland (1888). Must analyze which specific patent the alleged acquiescence relates to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction denied when patentability will be narrowly sustained if at all
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be denied where it is evident that the patent will be very narrowly sustained if at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Glaenzer v. Wiederer (1887). Weak validity prospects weigh against equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction denied where patentability or novelty is fairly contested
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will not issue where patentability is doubtful or the novelty of the invention is fairly contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Osborn v. Judd (1886); Upton v. Wayland (1888).

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction refused when other courts have decided no infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where infringement is doubtful, and other courts have decided that there is none, an injunction will be refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Thompson v. Rand-Avery Supply Co. (1889). Respect for prior adjudications in related jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past infringement not conclusive proof of future repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement in the past is not conclusive proof that the infringer will repeat the wrongful act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Proctor v. Bayley (L.R. 42 Ch. D. 390). Plaintiffs must show risk of recurrence to obtain injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction may issue though infringement has ceased if repetition likely
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will issue though infringement has ceased, if it can be repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. Arlington Mfg. Co. (1888); Facer v. Midvale Steel Works (1888). Preventive relief when future infringement probable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction may issue pre-use when device made for sale and advertised
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction may issue though no infringement has yet occurred; the court will act when the patented device has been made for sale and advertised though none have yet been used or sold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Buti Thermo-Electric Regulator Co. v. Jacobs Electric Co. (1888). Preparatory commercial acts can justify injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importing parts and failure to disclose purpose can warrant injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defendant has imported parts of the patented combination, and fails to disclose the purpose for which they are to be used, an injunction will issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Schneider v. Missouri Glass Co. (1888). Inference from opaque supply chain conduct can support relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final injunction only when final decree would favor plaintiff on same evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction ought not to be granted unless a final decree would be made for the plaintiff on the same evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Challender v. Royle (1887). Courts require likelihood of ultimate success before issuing permanent relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel of plaintiff due to acquiescence or laches
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the plaintiff has acquiesced in and countenanced the acts of the defendant an injunction will be refused; laches pending suit may also bar injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Amazeen Machine Co. v. Knight (1889); Pope Mfg. Co. v. Johnson (1889). Equity disfavors plaintiffs who wait to assert rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction refused to licensor who dealt unfairly to prejudice licensee
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be refused to a licensor who has dealt unfairly to the prejudice of the defendant licensee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Seibert Cylinder Oil Cup Co. v. Detroit Lubricator Co. (1888). Unclean hands and unfair dealing undermine equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-user due to state interference not ground to refuse injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-user because of State interference with the amount of royalties collectible is no ground for refusing an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: American Bell Telephone Co. v. Cushman Tel. & Service Co. (1888). State action that prevented exploitation does not necessarily forfeit equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest and defendant hardship can bar injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be refused when the defendant is solvent and has used the invention a long time without notice of infringement, and would suffer irreparable injury, and the public are benefited by his use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Root v. Mt. Adams & Eden Park Inclined R.R. Co. (1889). Consideration of public welfare and reliance interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: No injunction to prevent post-expiration use if articles wrongfully made before expiry and damages suit pending
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction to prevent the use or sale of articles after the expiration of the patent will not be allowed when the articles were wrongfully made before the patent expired, and a suit for damages therefor is pending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Westinghouse v. Carpenter (1888). Remedies for pre-expiration wrongdoing are damages rather than post-expiration injunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendee and user may be enjoined after maker enjoined elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: The vendee and user may be enjoined in one court after the maker has been enjoined in another, especially when the maker was not sued for the profits on this sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Thompson v. American Bank Note Co. (1888). Enjoining downstream actors is permissible to effect relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond in lieu of injunction when precedent/supreme decisions render patent doubtful
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond in lieu of an injunction will be ordered when former judgments sustaining the patent have been rendered doubtful by subsequent decisions of the Supreme Court, and the defendant would sustain irreparable injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Eastern Paper Bag Co. v. Nixon (1888). Equitable financial security can substitute for a prohibitory order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond and account in lieu of injunction when infringement disputed and defendant claims ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond and account may be ordered in lieu of an injunction when infringement is disputed, and defendant avers that he was ignorant of the patent until the suit was brought and derived no real aid from the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Eagle Mfg. Co. v. Chamberlain Plow Co. (1888). Fact-specific protective measures used when uncertainty exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of bill for injunction allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: It is proper to aver in a bill for an injunction that the patent has been established by judgments, to describe the patent generally, and make profert of it, and to allege infringement without specifying details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: American Bell Telephone Co. v. Southern Telephone Co. (1888). Pleading standards for seeking equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's bond liability for damages if injunction wrongful
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff gives bond on obtaining an injunction and fails in his suit he is liable on the bond for damages arising from loss of sales, depreciation of goods on hand, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Tobey Furniture Co. v. Colby (1888). Financial risk to plaintiffs who secure provisional relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction suspension rarely granted after judgment on merits
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will not be suspended after judgment on the merits, unless public interests are involved or large numbers of innocent persons would be injured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Consolidated Roller-Mill Co. v. Coombs (1889). Post-judgment stays limited to significant public hardship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contempt liability for failing to notify agents of injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: An enjoined defendant, neglecting to notify his agents of the injunction is liable in contempt for their violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Mundy v. Lidgerwood Mfg. Co. (1888). Defendants must take reasonable steps to prevent agent violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: No contempt adjudication when fair question of infringement exists under newly granted patent; plaintiff must sue
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an enjoined infringer acts under a patent granted since the decree and there is a fair question whether he infringes, he will not be adjudged in contempt on a motion, but the plaintiff must sue on the alleged infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Penna. Diamond Drill Co. v. Simpson (1889). Resolves conflict between contempt enforcement and substantive infringement claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominal penalty for non-wilful contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the contempt is not wilful a nominal fine and costs only will be imposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Morss v. Domestic Sewing Mach. Co. (1889). Courts tailor sanctions to culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner of Interferences exclusive jurisdiction over issues once declared
rubrics_metrics.description: The Examiner of Interferences has exclusive jurisdiction over the issues when declared, but none over the matter of patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Faure v. Bradley (1888). Distinguish interference issue jurisdiction from broader patentability review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign patent equivalence question rests with Examiner of Interferences
rubrics_metrics.description: The question whether a foreign patent covers the same invention as a domestic application in interference rests exclusively with the Examiner of Interferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Faure v. Bradley (1888). Office-level determination of cross-jurisdiction overlap in interference context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited review of examiner's interlocutory rulings
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision of the Examiner of Interferences on interlocutory motions will not be reviewed unless he abuses his discretion or disregards some rule of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Reynolds v. Haberman (1889). High deference to examiner's procedural rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference declared with unexpired patent only after rejection on that patent
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference will be declared with an unexpired patent only when the applicant has been rejected on that specific patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Ex parte Boyer (1889). Procedural prereq for interference declaration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent issued pending rival application treated as application in interference
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent issued pending a rival application is treated as an application also.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Ex parte Boyer (1889); Bechman v. Johnson (1889). Ensures parity between issued patents and pending applications for priority disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee has no interest in interference after patent issue to applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee has no interest in an interference proceeding after the question whether the applicant shall have a patent is determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Beardslee v. Moeslein (1889). Limits patentee involvement post-resolution of entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earlier application cannot benefit a different applicant unless same-applicant shown
rubrics_metrics.description: An earlier application cannot benefit the junior party to an interference unless it appear on its face or is proved by evidence to have been filed by the same applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Oliver v. Everitt (1889). Priority proof burden and documentary requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to dissolve interference limited to matters in application
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to dissolve an interference cannot be based on anything except the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Faure v. Bradley (1888). Scope of dissolution motions constrained to application record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference not dissolved for mere irregularity unless purpose defeated
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference will not be dissolved for irregularity unless it would defeat the purpose of the interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Steward v. Ellis (1889). Technical irregularities insufficient absent prejudice to core issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision on motion to dissolve that rests on merits precludes appeal to Commissioner
rubrics_metrics.description: If a decision on a motion to dissolve an interference rests on the merits, and not on the question whether an interference exists or whether the proceedings are so begun that this question can be decided, no appeal lies to the Commissioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Manny v. Easley (1889). Distinguish procedural vs merits-based dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference may be dissolved for non-patentability and remanded
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference may be dissolved on the ground of non-patentability and the case remanded after the time fixed by the rules where circumstances demand it, even though the same questions had been fully canvassed by the examiner before the interference was declared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Reynolds v. Haberman (1889). Patentability can terminate interference proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking testimony for Patent Office controlled by federal court where taken
rubrics_metrics.description: The matter of taking testimony for use in the Patent Office in interference cases is controlled by the Federal Court of the district where the evidence is taken, not by the Commissioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Wright v. Daggett (1888); Osgood v. Badger (1888). Procedural interplay between district courts and PTO in evidence collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositions in interference may be used in court if retaking impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: Depositions taken for the interference hearing between parties substantially the same may be used in court on a suit to annul if the same evidence cannot be retaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Clow v. Baker (1888). Preservation-of-testimony doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign invention evidence inadmissible in interference unless publication or patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of foreign invention is not admissible in an interference unless it be a publication or a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Green v. Hall (1889). Authentication and public availability required for foreign prior art in interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spousal incompetency as witnesses in Patent Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Husband and wife are not competent witnesses for or against each other in the Patent Office, which follows the law of the District of Columbia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Marsh v. Rein (1888). Witness competency rules affect available testimony in Office proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on later applicant claiming earlier was copied
rubrics_metrics.description: When a later applicant in interference claims that the earlier copied the invention from his, and that he is the true inventor and was using reasonable diligence in reducing, he has the burden of proof and must establish his claim by a fair preponderance of legal evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Wherry v. Heck (1889). Standard of proof for priority contests where derivation is alleged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence on interference between application and patent must be sufficient to overthrow patent in courts
rubrics_metrics.description: On an interference between an application and a patent, the evidence must be sufficient to overthrow the patent in the courts or obtain its repeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Beach v. Fowler (1889). Office proof standards mirror court invalidity thresholds for interference outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner may rehear predecessor's interference decisions where manifest error
rubrics_metrics.description: A Commissioner may rehear an interference case already decided by his predecessor in office; manifest error in law is ground for a rehearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Daniels v. Morgan (1889); Green v. Hall (1889). Rehearing available for legal error but limited where parties failed to try case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to prepare case precludes rehearing after judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: After judgment in interference a party who neglected to prepare and try his case cannot have a rehearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Beardslee v. Moeslein (1889). Sanctions neglect; diligence required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions for rehearing by different parties should be heard together
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions for a rehearing by different parties to an interference should all be made and heard together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Green v. Hall (1889). Procedural efficiency and fairness in rehearing practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment in interference conclusive according to court's construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgment in interference concludes the issues according to the construction put upon them by the court, and parties who acquiesce in such judgment cannot be allowed afterward to claim for it a different effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Ex parte Gray (1889). Finality of construction and estoppel by acquiescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner bound by judgment in interference
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner is concluded by a judgment in interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Ex parte Booth (1889). Effect of judicial determinations on subsequent Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party may later deny patentability in courts
rubrics_metrics.description: A party to an interference may subsequently deny patentability in the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Holliday v. Pickhardt (1887). Office positions on entitlement do not forever preclude later invalidity challenges in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal from examiner's no-interference or dissolution decision lies to Commissioner
rubrics_metrics.description: From a decision of an examiner that no interference exists, and that those declared must be dissolved, an appeal lies to the Commissioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Von Welsbach v. Lungren (1889). Appellate path in Office proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: No appeal to Commissioner from examiner's dissolution decision involving right to make claim
rubrics_metrics.description: No appeal lies to the Commissioner from a decision of the examiner on a motion to dissolve an interference involving the right of one of the parties to make the claim in issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Steward v. Ellis (1889). Limited appellate jurisdiction over certain claim-right disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal may be signed nunc pro tunc
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal may be signed by the attorney nunc pro tunc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Pitney v. Smith (1889). Procedural flexibility for appeal formalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of reasons for appeal is not part of appeal and may be amended
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement of the reasons for appeal on an interference is no part of the appeal itself and if omitted or defective the appeal may still be valid, and the statement afterward supplied or amended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Pitney v. Smith (1889). Substance of appeal is controlling; supporting statements are amendable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely appeal cannot be deemed for delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an appeal is seasonably taken the Commissioner cannot decide that it is taken for purposes of delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Pitney v. Smith (1889). Courts respect timely procedural rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue of patent to prevailing interference party not delayed by bill in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: The issue of a patent to the party prevailing in an interference cannot be delayed by the filing of a bill in equity by the defeated party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Wells v. Boyle (1888). Office issuance proceeds despite collateral equity filings by losers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreasonable delay by one applicant cannot delay action on contestants
rubrics_metrics.description: The unreasonable delay of one applicant in pursuing his rights cannot operate to delay action on contesting applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Ex parte Lombard (1888). Docket management and fairness to other parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of a natural force can be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: The application of a natural force may be a patentable invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. Frederick Crane Chemical Co. (1888). Process of using natural forces can be eligible if new and useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small advance toward existing trend may be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention reached by taking the one step in advance toward which the art was tending is new and patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Anilin v. LeTinstem (1887). Incremental improvements can be patentable when nonobvious relative to prior trend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of business method of soliciting customers not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of a method of soliciting custom is not an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Bristol v. Equitable Life Assurance Soc. (1889). Abstract business concepts without technical implementation not patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery essential to patentability alongside novelty and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery is essential to patentability as well as novelty and utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Ex parte Devin (1888); Ex parte Gifford (1888). Mere identification of natural phenomena without discovery may be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention must be product of original conception
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be the product of an original conception, not merely the carrying forward of an original idea in degree, nor combining old devices without a new mode of operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Burt v. Every (1890). Nonobviousness requires more than predictable variation or aggregation of prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive skill implies more than mere changes in form/arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive skill implies more than change of form, proportion, degree, use, or arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Worswick Mfg. Co. v. City of Kansas (1889). Substance-over-form test for inventive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive skill requires thought distinct from mechanical skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive skill requires thought; mechanical skill does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Butler v. Bainbridge (1886). Distinguish routine implementation from true inventive reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor must be able to perceive, reproduce, and communicate invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor must perceive and be able to reproduce his invention and to communicate it to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: McDonough v. Gray (1889). Enablement and possession aspects of inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coincidence of conclusions suggests mechanical not inventive skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Coincidence in the conclusions of two or more alleged inventors indicates mechanical rather than inventive skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Falls Rivet Co. v. Wolfe (1889). Independent simultaneous derivation may indicate predictable, non-inventive solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to previously produce long-needed means supports inventive skill when produced and adopted
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to produce a long-needed and instantly accepted means shows that when produced it resulted from inventive skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. American Zylonite Co. (1888). Commercial adoption bolsters evidence of nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beneficial improvement and cost reduction indicate inventive skill
rubrics_metrics.description: A different and beneficial suit, improving and cheapening the product, indicates that the change in the mode of production involved inventive skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Zinsser v. Kremer (1889). Economic and practical advantages are probative of inventive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate adoption evidences novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The immediate adoption of a means which supplies a long-felt want indicates novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: United Nickel Co. v. California Electrical Works (1885). Market uptake as corroborating novelty/inventive value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public acceptance is evidence of patentability and inventive skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance by the public is evidence of patentability and indicates inventive skill; immediate acceptance may be better evidence than expert opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Tondeur v. Chambers (1889); Shipman Engine Co. v. Rochester Tool Works (1888); Palmer v. Johnston (1888). Commercial success used as objective indicium of nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earliest reducer favored by law
rubrics_metrics.description: The earliest reducer is favored by the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Green v. Hall (1889). Emphasis on diligence in reduction to practice for priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on employer claiming joint invention against employee's sole patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof is on an employer claiming joint invention against the sole patent of the employee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Locke v. Lane & Bodley Co. (1888). Employers asserting joint inventorship must present affirmative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: One joint patentee may later file sole application and is not estopped
rubrics_metrics.description: One of two joint patentees may afterward file a sole application and have an interference declared with the joint patent, and is not estopped by his former joint oath nor barred by a previous assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Kohler v. Kohler (1888). Complexities of changing inventorship claims and estoppel limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Former sworn statements can neutralize later testimony claiming sole inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The testimony of one of two joint patentees that he was in fact a sole inventor is neutralized by his former oath taken to obtain the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Schlicht & Field Co. v. Chicago Sewing-Machine Co. (1888). Prior inconsistent statements carry evidentiary weight against later claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisions of higher courts followed absent new evidence; may be departed from if facts differ
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions of the Supreme and Circuit Courts will be followed where there is no new evidence, but a judgment of the Supreme Court may be departed from when the facts are different; prior judgments between other parties and on other facts may also be departed from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: American Bell Telephone Co. v. Wallace Electric Tel. Co. (1889); American Bell Telephone Co. v. Southern Telephone Co. (1888); Worswick Mfg. Co. v. City of Kansas (1889). Precedent is persuasive but fact-sensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comity: follow co-ordinate court judgments where issues and evidence same
rubrics_metrics.description: Comity requires a judgment in a co-ordinate court in favor of validity to be followed where issues and evidence are the same, but one Circuit will not reverse its own decisions out of deference to another, and comity does not require following a decision after the Supreme Court has defined points more strictly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Hancock Inspirator Co. v. Regester (1888); Consolidated Boiler Mill Co. v. George T. Smith Middlings Purifier Co. (1889); Rubber & Celluloid Harness Trimming Co. v. India Rubber Comb Co. (1888). Respect for co-ordinate decisions tempered by court independence and subsequent higher-court clarification.
